name: Foundations Bank (translated)
desc: 79 Foundations practice items from a Spanish community prep set, adapted to English — single- and multiple-response concept checks across all five domains. 60 drawn per sitting.
source: Questions and rationales: https://github.com/juanmartincoma-collab/claude-certified-architect-es by Juan Martín Cordero ("Claude Certified Architect — preparación en español", v1.0.0, commit 02e8b16), Foundations (CCAR-F) items from the simulator bank. Rationales translated from Spanish to English and adapted to this format: option order shuffled, "Select N" added to multiple-response stems, distractor reasons rewritten to name options instead of letters. 20 items out of scope for this bank or with disputed answers, and all 11 matching-grid items, were omitted.
licence: "Claude Certified Architect — preparación en español" by Juan Martín Cordero, https://github.com/juanmartincoma-collab/claude-certified-architect-es, is licensed under CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes made: Foundations items selected; explanations translated from Spanish to English and reworded to reference option text; option order shuffled; difficulty, domain and scenario tags reassigned; matching-grid, out-of-scope and disputed items removed. This adaptation is not endorsed by the original author. The original work is unofficial and not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic PBC; "Claude" and "Claude Certified Architect" are trademarks of Anthropic PBC.

questions.q: A fixed workflow for supplier onboarding now fails on roughly a fifth of cases, where staff step in manually to finish the job. Which TWO signals would justify moving this stage to an autonomous agent? (Select 2)
options: The manual interventions follow no repeatable pattern the team can list
The steps differ per supplier and only become clear part-way through
The number of onboarding requests per week has roughly doubled since launch
Leadership wants the solution to look more advanced to the board
The cost per request has risen along with the added volume
questions.explain: Autonomy is justified when the path cannot be listed in advance. Interventions that follow no listable pattern, and steps that only appear part-way through, are exactly that condition. Doubled volume and rising cost are scale and cost problems that any pattern can absorb; wanting the solution to look advanced to the board is prestige, not an architectural driver.

questions.q: A supervisor coordinates four specialist agents in a regulated claims process. Which TWO responsibilities belong to the supervisor rather than to the specialists? (Select 2)
options: Formatting each specialist's own output for its internal use
Applying the rules that determine whether a claim is fraudulent
Recording the ordered outcome of every step for the audit trail
Deciding the order the specialists run in and when to stop the chain
Choosing which model version each specialist should call at runtime
questions.explain: The supervisor supplies sequencing and a single point where the order of decisions is recorded — exactly what a peer-to-peer arrangement cannot guarantee. Applying the fraud rules is the specialist's job; formatting a specialist's own output is internal to that agent; choosing model versions is configuration fixed in advance, not runtime orchestration.

questions.q: An architect is splitting a long analysis task into sequenced subtasks. Which TWO practices make the decomposition real rather than cosmetic? (Select 2)
options: Merging the steps back into one call once quality has improved
Running each of the steps on the largest model in the family
Passing structured output between steps so each one can be checked
Giving every step only the context that step actually needs
Keeping the original prompt intact and appending the steps
questions.explain: Decomposition pays off for two reasons: each step gets focused attention, and each intermediate output can be checked. Without structured output between steps the chain is a black box again. Running every step on the largest model confuses capability with structure; keeping the original prompt intact and appending steps leaves the giant prompt in place; merging the steps back into one call undoes the decomposition.

questions.q: Which TWO conditions indicate that a single augmented model call is enough, with no workflow or agent around it? (Select 2)
options: Each step has to be recorded separately for an external auditor
Several specialists must contribute before the output is complete
Any reference material needed fits alongside the request itself
The next step depends entirely on what the previous step happened to return
The task is one transformation whose context can be supplied up front
questions.explain: A single augmented call is enough when there is one transformation and the context it needs fits alongside the request. It is the lowest rung of the ladder and is chosen whenever it suffices. Several contributing specialists call for multi-agent; a next step that depends entirely on what the previous one returned calls for a workflow or an agent; separately recorded steps for an auditor call for a workflow with discrete steps.

questions.q: Which TWO practices make the guardrails written into a system prompt more likely to hold? (Select 2)
options: Pasting the full guardrail list, unchanged, into every section of the prompt
Writing the guardrails in a noticeably more emphatic and commanding tone
Placing the guardrails at the start or end, apart from reference material
Assuming the guardrail also covers the cases it does not mention
Stating explicitly what takes precedence when two instructions conflict
questions.explain: Two real levers: an explicit statement of which instruction wins when two conflict, and placing the guardrails away from the middle of the context, structurally separate from reference material. A more emphatic tone is superstition, not a mechanism; pasting the whole list into every section inflates and dilutes the prompt; assuming a guardrail covers cases it does not mention is an assumption, not a practice.

questions.q: A support agent has a tool that can delete customer records. Which TWO changes reduce the blast radius without removing the capability from the platform? (Select 2)
options: Require an explicit approval step before any delete call executes
Rename the tool so the model is less likely to select it by mistake
Scope the tool's credentials so it can only reach the support dataset
Add the word 'careful' to the tool description so that the model hesitates
Log every delete after the fact so the team can review them weekly
questions.explain: Least privilege plus a gate before the irreversible action: scoped credentials limit what the tool can reach, and the approval step requires a human before it executes. Adding 'careful' to the description or renaming the tool are text nudges, not controls; logging deletes for a weekly review is detection after the record is already gone.

questions.q: An architect is choosing between MCP and direct API integration for a new internal system. Which TWO facts about the situation point to MCP? (Select 2)
options: Only the data engineering team will ever query this system directly
The system is only ever queried by one service the team owns
The team owning the system will keep adding and retiring endpoints
Three separate AI applications will need the same access to this system
The integration is a single deterministic call inside a nightly job
questions.explain: MCP pays off when there are several consumers and the catalogue changes often: the owning team maintains its server once and every client reuses it, picking up new tools when it connects. A single deterministic call in a nightly job, one owned service, or a single querying team all describe one stable consumer — the case where a direct integration is simpler.

questions.q: A team wants to expose forty internal endpoints to an agent. Tool-selection accuracy in testing drops sharply past roughly a dozen tools. What is the sound design response?
options: Group the endpoints into task-oriented tools and load them on demand
Expose one generic tool that accepts the endpoint name as a parameter
Register all forty and instruct the model to think before selecting one
Register all forty tools and rely on a more capable model to choose
questions.explain: Tools are designed around tasks, not as a mirror of the internal API, and only the ones relevant to a request are presented. The complexity stays on the system side, where it is deterministic. A more capable model buys capability without reducing the confusion; telling the model to think first adds latency to every call without shrinking the choice; one generic tool taking the endpoint name throws away typed interfaces and makes errors harder to catch.

questions.q: A platform team is enabling AI-assisted development across twelve squads. Which TWO measures scale the practice without scaling the risk? (Select 2)
options: Let each squad publish its own standards independently
Define which commands automated tooling may run and on which branches
Grant the tooling broad credentials so squads are never blocked
Keep shared configuration and prompt standards under version control
Adopt every new assistant tool in the week it becomes available
questions.explain: Accelerator and brake at once: proven practice that every squad inherits through version control, and explicit limits on what automation may execute. Broad credentials maximise the blast radius; letting each squad publish its own standards recreates fragmentation; adopting every new tool in its first week adds churn without evaluation.

questions.q: Reviews of AI-authored pull requests almost never raise findings, yet defects keep reaching production. What is the most likely cause?
options: The reviewer shares the context and assumptions that produced the code
The model used for the review is smaller than the one used for authoring
The review prompt is too short to describe what quality means here
The team merges before the automated review has finished running
questions.explain: A reviewer anchored to the reasoning that produced the code inherits its blind spots, so review should come from a fresh context separate from the authoring session. A longer review prompt or a different model size are configuration tweaks that leave the anchoring untouched; merging before the review finishes would be a process problem visible in the timings, not a reason for reviews that run and find nothing.

questions.q: A team wants every session in a repository to follow the same commit-message convention. Which mechanism is the right home for that rule?
options: An entry in settings.json under the permissions block
A CLAUDE.md file committed at the root of the repository
A PreToolUse hook that inspects and rejects the commit message
A slash command each developer runs before committing
questions.explain: A style convention is a reasonable request, not a hard guarantee: it belongs in CLAUDE.md, which the model reads and generally follows, committed so the whole team inherits it. A PreToolUse hook is a hard mechanism for something that does not need one and is costly to maintain; settings.json permissions do not configure behaviour; a slash command depends on someone remembering to run it.

questions.q: A rule must hold without exception: no command may ever touch the production database. Which mechanism enforces it?
options: A PreToolUse hook that inspects the command and exits with code 2
A comment in the codebase next to the connection string
A prominent warning placed at the top of the project's CLAUDE.md file
A slash command that wraps the safe version of the query
questions.explain: 'Without exception' demands a hard mechanism. The hook runs before the tool, is deterministic code, and exiting with code 2 blocks the call and returns the reason to the model. A CLAUDE.md warning, a wrapping slash command and a code comment are all text: followed almost always, which is not the same as always.

questions.q: Of these hook events, which can stop a tool call before it runs?
options: SessionStart
PreCompact
PreToolUse
PostToolUse
questions.explain: Only PreToolUse fires before the tool runs and can block it (exit code 2 or a deny decision). PostToolUse runs after the call has completed, so it can format or record the result but not prevent it; SessionStart loads state when a session opens and PreCompact preserves context before compaction, and neither is tied to a tool call.

questions.q: A PreToolUse hook exits with code 2 after a blocked command. Which TWO things happen next? (Select 2)
options: What the hook wrote to stderr goes back to the model
The tool call never executes
The session ends and has to be restarted by the user
The model retries the same command automatically
PostToolUse still runs so the block can be recorded
questions.explain: The block is not a silent lock: it prevents execution and feeds the explanation (stderr) back to the model, which can change course in the same turn. Ending the session is far too drastic and does not happen; PostToolUse does not run because no tool ran; the model is not made to retry automatically — it decides what to do with the explanation it received.

questions.q: A developer writes a personal preference into settings.local.json while the team's version sits in settings.json. Which one applies to that developer?
options: Neither, until the developer restarts the whole session
The versioned file, because the team's setting is shared
The local file, because the more specific layer wins
Both merge, with conflicting keys raising an error
questions.explain: Settings resolve in layers and the more specific one wins, so the developer's settings.local.json overrides the shared settings.json. The exception is permissions, where the most restrictive rule wins: a deny stays a deny even if another layer allows it. 'The shared file wins' inverts the precedence; conflicting keys do not raise an error; a restart has nothing to do with how layers resolve.

questions.q: An API key is needed by a project's MCP server. Where does it belong?
options: An environment variable referenced by the configuration
The versioned .mcp.json file, so the whole team shares it
The project CLAUDE.md, so the model knows to use it
A slash command that pastes it when it is needed
questions.explain: A secret never goes in a version-controlled file or anywhere the model reads. It lives in an environment variable that the configuration references. Putting it in the committed .mcp.json publishes it in the repository; putting it in CLAUDE.md puts it in the context window; a slash command that pastes it exposes it on every invocation.

questions.q: What exactly does a project's .mcp.json do?
options: Stores the instructions the model should follow per server
Records which servers each developer prefers to enable
Declares which MCP servers exist and how to connect to them
Grants the permissions that those MCP servers are allowed to use
questions.explain: It does one thing: declare which MCP servers exist and how to connect to them. It does not grant permissions (that is settings.json), hold instructions for the model (that would be CLAUDE.md), store secrets, or record per-developer preferences (that is user scope, not project scope).

questions.q: A monorepo holds twelve applications, each with its own conventions. Which TWO practices keep context usage sane? (Select 2)
options: Concatenate every app's conventions into the single root file for clarity
Put app-specific conventions in a CLAUDE.md inside each app folder
Ask developers to paste the relevant conventions at session start
Keep only shared, repo-wide conventions in the root CLAUDE.md
Move all conventions into settings.json so they load on demand
questions.explain: A CLAUDE.md in a subfolder loads on demand, only when files in that folder are touched, which avoids dragging twelve applications' conventions into every session; the root file keeps only what is shared. Concatenating everything into the root file is exactly the waste to avoid; settings.json holds configuration, not instructions; asking developers to paste conventions depends on human memory.

questions.q: A pull-request review runs headless in CI. Which setting keeps the run reproducible across builds?
options: An interactive approval step for any command outside the allowlist
A fresh session for every job, with permissions declared up front
An unbounded turn limit so the review is never cut short midway
A long-lived session reused across jobs to keep context
questions.explain: In CI nobody is watching: every decision a human would have made on the fly must be made before the run starts, and a fresh session per job stops two identical inputs from producing different results. A long-lived session makes each result depend on history; an interactive approval step hangs the pipeline; an unbounded turn limit leaves both the run and the bill without a ceiling.

questions.q: An automated review should block a merge when it finds a critical issue. Where does the blocking decision belong?
options: In the model, which decides whether the issue warrants a block
In pipeline code applying a rule to the model's structured findings
In a PostToolUse hook that inspects the review output right afterwards
In the reviewer's judgement after reading the model's summary
questions.explain: Automated review informs a decision rather than replacing it: the model returns structured findings with severities and pipeline code applies a deterministic rule. Letting the model decide puts a gate decision in non-deterministic hands; a PostToolUse hook runs after the fact and does not block a merge; a human reading a summary is valid but is neither automated nor deterministic.

questions.q: Which TWO statements about hook security are accurate? (Select 2)
options: A hook runs locally with the user's own permissions, without asking
Hooks require explicit confirmation from the user on every trigger
Hooks can only execute commands that appear in the allow list
A hook from an untrusted repository is arbitrary code execution
Hooks run inside a sandbox that isolates them from the whole file system
questions.explain: A hook runs on the local machine, with the user's own permissions and automatically when its event fires, so accepting an untrusted repository's hook configuration amounts to running someone else's code. Sandboxing, per-trigger confirmation and allow-list-only execution describe protections hooks do not have — which is why hook configuration must be reviewed before it is accepted.

questions.q: A team wants a procedure the model invokes on its own when the situation calls for it, without anyone typing a command. Which mechanism fits?
options: A skill, selected by the model from its description
A slash command the developer types when needed
An entry appended to the end of the project CLAUDE.md file
A hook bound to the tool the procedure relates to
questions.explain: Skills, slash commands and hooks are all saved procedures; they differ in who decides to use them. The model chooses a skill by reading its description, which is why the description is the most important part of a skill. A slash command is invoked by a person; a hook is fired by the system on a tool event; a CLAUDE.md entry is a standing instruction, not an invocable procedure.

questions.q: A long research task keeps filling the main session with raw output that is only needed once. Which mechanism protects the context?
options: Add a PreCompact hook that trims the output before compaction
Load a skill that explains how to do the research more efficiently
Delegate the work to a subagent that returns only the conclusion
Raise the turn limit so the session can absorb more material
questions.explain: A subagent has its own context window: it takes the mess into its own context and returns only the conclusion. A skill, by contrast, feeds instructions into the main model's own context and isolates nothing. A PreCompact hook acts only once the context has already filled; raising the turn limit makes the problem bigger instead of avoiding it.

questions.q: Which TWO facts about permissions in settings.json are correct? (Select 2)
options: Allow lists are advisory and the model may override them if needed
A deny rule beats an allow rule from any other configuration layer
Permissions are inherited only when the project has no local file
Rules are written per tool and can use patterns to narrow scope
The model reads the permission list and explains its choices from it
questions.explain: Permissions are a hard mechanism: rules are declared per tool, with patterns to narrow them, and a deny always wins. Rules are enforced by the harness, not by the model reading a list: a denied call is simply refused when attempted. So 'the model reads the list and explains from it' is false, 'allow lists are advisory' contradicts the mechanism, and 'inherited only when there is no local file' misdescribes the layering.

questions.q: A report needs four independent sections researched and then written as one document. How should the work be split across agents?
options: Four subagents each research and write their own section
A single agent researches and then writes everything in one long pass
Four subagents research in parallel, one agent writes the document
Four subagents write, and a fifth merges their four drafts
questions.explain: Parallelise the fieldwork, not the writing. Voice, narrative thread and avoiding repetition are properties of the whole document, and no individual subagent can see them. Four subagents each writing their own section, or four drafts merged by a fifth, both produce four voices and overlaps; a single agent doing everything wastes the available parallelism.

questions.q: An orchestrator dispatches subagents whose number is only known once the problem is read. Which pattern is this?
options: Routing across a fixed menu
Parallelization over fixed sections
Orchestrator–workers
Prompt chaining in a fixed sequence
questions.explain: In orchestrator–workers, the subtasks are created on reading the problem and the orchestrator's main job is the final synthesis. Routing chooses one path from options that already exist; parallelisation splits sections defined in advance; prompt chaining is a fixed sequential chain. None of those fits a number of workers that is only known at runtime.

questions.q: A subagent receives its assignment from an orchestrator. Which TWO parts of that assignment should a person define in advance, not the orchestrator at runtime? (Select 2)
options: The specific question this subagent must answer
The portion of the problem it has been given
The hard limits and the tools it may use
The order in which it should consult its sources
The output format every subagent must return
questions.explain: The person fixes the contract; the model fills in the content. Without a common output format the results cannot be combined, and hard limits and permitted tools are safety decisions, not content decisions. The specific question, the slice of the problem and the order of sources all depend on the concrete problem and can only be decided at runtime.

questions.q: One of five subagents fails and returns nothing. What should the orchestrator do?
options: Abort the whole run and return an error to the user
Deliver the four results and state which part is missing
Deliver the four results as though the whole set were complete
Retry the failed subagent until it eventually succeeds
questions.explain: Honest degradation: deliver what you have and state what is missing. Presenting four results as if they were five is lying by omission; aborting the whole run discards four valid results; retrying until success may never terminate.

questions.q: A team is deciding whether a multi-agent design is worth its overhead. Which TWO conditions make it pay off? (Select 2)
options: The team wants the architecture to look more capable to the client
Several subtasks must run in a strict order, each using the last result
The subtasks are independent and do not need to talk to each other
Two agents need to read and update the same shared state as they go
Each subtask produces bulk material that is better summarised apart
questions.explain: Multi-agent systems use on the order of fifteen times more tokens than a normal chat, so the design pays only with genuinely independent subtasks and subtasks that generate bulk material worth summarising separately. Strict sequential dependency and shared mutable state are precisely where multi-agent designs fail; wanting the architecture to look capable is not an architectural criterion.

questions.q: An agent can send emails to customers on its own. Where does the checkpoint belong?
options: Before the send, as a confirmation the agent cannot bypass
After the send, with a notification to the account owner
Inside the prompt, as an instruction to confirm before sending
Nowhere: the agent already drafts within approved templates
questions.explain: Sending is irreversible and leaves the organisation, so it needs a confirmation or verifiable rule the agent cannot bypass — never the model's own judgement inside the prompt. A prompt instruction to confirm leaves the guarantee to an instruction; a notification after the send warns only after the damage; approved templates control the wording, not whether the send should happen.

questions.q: Results from parallel subagents come back in incompatible shapes and cannot be combined. Which TWO fixes address the cause? (Select 2)
options: Increase each subagent's context so it can see all the others' work
Define one output contract that every subagent must fill in
Validate each subagent's return against that contract before use
Ask the orchestrator to reformat whatever each subagent sent
Run the subagents sequentially so later ones copy the first
questions.explain: Mismatched shapes mean the human-written output contract is missing. Define it once and validate each return against it before trying to combine anything. Having the orchestrator reformat whatever arrives patches the symptom downstream; letting each subagent see the others' work breaks the isolation that justifies subagents; running them sequentially sacrifices the parallelism.

questions.q: A downstream service parses the model's output as JSON and crashes when a field is missing. What is the correct fix?
options: Enforce the shape with a schema instead of asking for it in the prompt
Post-process the text with a regular expression to patch the gaps
Add a sentence to the prompt insisting the JSON must be complete
Wrap the parser in a try block and skip records that fail
questions.explain: If a program consumes the output, its structure is enforced with a schema, not requested in the prompt. Asking works almost always, and almost always is not enough when a parser sits on the other end. A firmer sentence in the prompt is still a request; wrapping the parser and skipping failures turns the error into a silent loss of records; regex patching treats symptoms and accumulates debt.

questions.q: A prompt mixes instructions, a reference document and a user question, and the model keeps confusing them. What is the most direct improvement?
options: Delimit each part with explicit tags so the boundaries are unambiguous
Shorten the reference document until the confusion disappears
Raise the temperature so that the model interprets the layout more loosely
Repeat the instructions again after the reference document ends
questions.explain: When the model mixes the parts up, the problem is that there is no explicit boundary. Delimiting with tags separates instruction, data and question without changing the content. Repeating the instructions inflates the prompt without marking the boundaries; shortening the document discards material the task needs; a higher temperature only increases variability.

questions.q: An extraction step returns valid JSON that occasionally contains a wrong value. Which TWO responses fit? (Select 2)
options: Validate the values against business rules, not just against the shape
Log the discrepancy and pass the record downstream unchanged
Fall back to an empty object whenever the validation step does not pass it
Return the failure explicitly so the caller can decide what to do
Retry the same call repeatedly until a valid value comes back
questions.explain: Well-formed JSON can still be wrong in content: validate it against business rules and, if it fails, make the failure visible to the caller. A silent failure contaminates data and is discovered late. Falling back to an empty object and logging-then-passing-through are both silent failures in different clothes; retrying the identical call repeatedly changes nothing that would fix the value.

questions.q: An output will be read by a person, not parsed by a program. What follows for its format?
options: A schema should still be enforced for consistency across responses
Prose is fine; a strict schema adds cost without buying anything
The output should be JSON so it can be reused programmatically later
The format should change per request to suit the reader's preference
questions.explain: The question that organises this domain is who consumes the output. For a person, a format slip breaks nothing, and putting a hard mechanism where a soft one suffices costs maintenance and buys nothing. Enforcing a schema anyway, or emitting JSON for hypothetical reuse, over-corrects; changing the format per request makes the behaviour unpredictable.

questions.q: Few-shot examples were added to a classification prompt and accuracy on one rare category got worse. What is the likely cause?
options: The temperature is too low for the examples to have any influence
The examples are too short for the model to learn the whole pattern from
Few-shot prompting does not work for classification tasks at all
The examples over-represent the common categories and skew the model
questions.explain: Examples are the implicit specification of the task. If their distribution does not reflect the real categories, the model learns that imbalance and the rare category suffers. Blaming example length or temperature attributes the failure to parameters rather than to what the examples teach; few-shot prompting does work for classification, so 'it never works' is false.

questions.q: A tool wraps an internal API with eleven optional parameters. The agent fills them inconsistently. What is the better design?
options: Add validation that rejects calls with unusual parameter combinations
Let the agent send free-form text and parse the parameters out of it
Document all eleven parameters more thoroughly in the description
Expose a task-oriented tool that takes only what the task needs
questions.explain: Tools are designed around the task, not as a mirror of the internal API; the complexity stays on the system side, where it is deterministic and testable. Documenting all eleven parameters more thoroughly moves the burden into the context; validation that rejects odd combinations catches the symptom; free-form text parsed afterwards throws away the typed interface.

questions.q: A tool returns an empty list when the underlying service times out. What is wrong with that?
options: Timeouts should always be retried inside the tool without informing anyone
Empty lists are valid only when the query itself was malformed
The empty list uses more tokens than an explicit error would use
The model reads it as 'no results' and answers confidently from nothing
questions.explain: This is the cardinal anti-pattern: returning empty on an error is a silent failure. The model concludes there are no results and builds a confident answer on a false premise. The token count is irrelevant; retrying silently inside the tool hides the problem one layer lower; an empty list on a malformed query does not describe the defect here, which is an access failure dressed up as a valid empty result.

questions.q: Which TWO properties make a tool description effective? (Select 2)
options: It uses the same wording as the other tools for consistency
It states plainly when the tool should and should not be used
It names the boundary with the tools closest to it in purpose
It lists every error code that the underlying service can return
It documents the internal implementation the tool wraps
questions.explain: The description is the whole interface: it is the only thing the model has to decide with. Saying when to use the tool and how it differs from its nearest neighbours is exactly what prevents wrong selections. Documenting the internal implementation or every error code fills context with detail that does not change the decision; copying the neighbours' wording is cosmetic and can increase confusion.

questions.q: A long agent session degrades as it goes: earlier facts get dropped and answers drift. What is the sound response?
options: Start over from scratch each time the drift becomes noticeable
Re-inject the facts that must survive, instead of trusting the history
Ask the model to summarise the conversation and continue
Increase the temperature so the model explores the history more
questions.explain: The organising question is whether a piece of information must survive no matter what. If so, it cannot live only in the conversation: it is re-injected. Asking the model to summarise and carry on loses detail and still depends on the history; temperature has nothing to do with it; starting over discards useful work.

questions.q: An agent loop needs to know when the task is actually finished. Which signal is the reliable one?
options: A stop_reason of end_turn on the model's response
A stop_reason of max_tokens once the budget is spent
An assistant message that contains no text blocks
A stop_reason of tool_use with no tools left to run
questions.explain: end_turn is the signal that the model has finished its turn. The loop is: send, inspect stop_reason, run tools if it says tool_use, append the results, repeat. tool_use means the model asked for a tool, so the loop must continue; a message with no text blocks is not a protocol signal; max_tokens means the response was cut off, not that it finished. Current docs: other stop reasons such as pause_turn, refusal and model_context_window_exceeded also exist, but end_turn is still the normal finish signal.

questions.q: A tool has finished executing. How does its result get back to the model?
options: Injected into the system prompt for the following request
Stored server-side and referenced later by the tool call identifier
Returned as a new assistant message the model then reads
Appended as a user-role message containing tool_result blocks
questions.explain: Results go back as a user-role message containing tool_result blocks, and every request resends the full history — there is no server-side state. Injecting results into the system prompt or returning them as an assistant message puts them in the wrong role; storing them server-side assumes persistence the API does not provide.

questions.q: A coordinator issues several Task calls inside a single response. What happens?
options: The call fails as ambiguous
They queue and run one after another
They execute in parallel
Only the first one is executed
questions.explain: Several Task calls in one response run in parallel; that is the lever for spreading independent fieldwork. Queuing them one after another, running only the first, or failing as ambiguous do not happen — parallelism is precisely why you group the calls into one response. Current docs: the Task tool is now named Agent; Task remains an alias.

questions.q: Which TWO situations call for starting a fresh session rather than continuing the current one? (Select 2)
options: A long stretch of unrelated work has degraded the working context
You want to try an alternative approach from the same point in the task
The next task needs the same repository and the same conventions
The tool results in context are stale and no longer reflect reality
The conversation is long but every earlier fact is still accurate
questions.explain: Start a fresh session when the context is no longer trustworthy: stale tool results, or degradation after unrelated work. Needing the same repository and conventions is no reason to cut; trying an alternative approach from the same point in the task is what forking a session is for, not starting from scratch; a long conversation whose facts are all still accurate is a healthy context.

questions.q: A refund above a fixed threshold must never be issued without approval. Where does that rule belong?
options: In the tool description, so the model knows the limit
In a PreToolUse hook that blocks the call deterministically
In the system prompt, written as a clearly worded operating rule
In the escalation guidance the agent reads before acting
questions.explain: Financial and compliance rules are guaranteed with a deterministic mechanism. A text instruction is probabilistic — it works almost always, and almost always is not enough when money is involved. The system prompt, the tool description and the escalation guidance are all variations of the same text: they ask, they do not prevent.

questions.q: A review process must analyse each file locally and then check consistency across files. Which decomposition fits?
options: A fixed pipeline that reviews files in alphabetical order once
A single pass that loads every file and reasons over all of them at once
A multi-pass design: one pass per file, then an integration pass
One subagent per file, each also judging cross-file consistency
questions.explain: A single pass over many files dilutes attention and applies the criteria unevenly. A per-file pass handles local issues and an integration pass handles what is only visible across files. One pass over everything is the anti-pattern; one subagent per file judging cross-file consistency asks each subagent for something it cannot see; an alphabetical fixed pipeline does not separate the two levels of analysis.

questions.q: New team members keep missing the project's coding standards, which live in the lead's own CLAUDE.md. What is the fix?
options: Ask each new member to copy the lead's file into their home directory
Move them to a project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repository
Paste the standards into the first message of every new session
Move them into settings.json so the tooling enforces them directly
questions.explain: This is the classic misconfiguration: team instructions stored at user level. What the whole team must see goes in the project file, committed to the repository. Copying the lead's file into each home directory does not scale and drifts out of sync; pasting standards into each session depends on memory; settings.json holds configuration, not instructions the model reads.

questions.q: A CLAUDE.md pulls in other files with the @path import syntax. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select 2)
options: Imports accept a space between the @ and the path for readability
Only Markdown files can be imported, never configuration files
Relative paths resolve against the file doing the importing
Imported files load only when the model explicitly asks for them
Imports can nest, but only up to a maximum depth of four hops
questions.explain: Relative paths resolve against the importing file, and nesting is capped at four hops; imports are for splitting long conventions into maintainable pieces. Imports load with the CLAUDE.md that references them, not only when the model asks; there is no space between the @ and the path; and non-Markdown files such as a README or package.json can be imported.

questions.q: A team moves its conventions from one long CLAUDE.md into .claude/rules/ files with paths frontmatter. Which TWO gains does that produce? (Select 2)
options: Each rule loads only when files matching its patterns are touched
All conventions load at session start, which speeds up responses
Rules become enforceable, so the model can no longer ignore any of them
Context and tokens are spent only on the conventions in play
The rules apply to every repository the developer works in
questions.explain: paths frontmatter activates each rule only when matching files are touched — progressive disclosure applied to conventions, so context is spent only on the conventions in play. Rules are still text, so they do not become enforceable; they do not all load at session start (that is the opposite of what happens); applying to every repository describes user scope, not project rules.

questions.q: A skill produces very verbose output that pollutes the main session. Which frontmatter setting addresses it?
options: allowed-tools, so the skill touches fewer files overall
context: fork, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent
A shorter description, so it is invoked less often
argument-hint, so the skill asks for narrower input
questions.explain: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent: the noise stays in its own window and the main context stays clean. allowed-tools pre-approves the tools the skill may use, it does not change how much output lands in the main session; argument-hint improves usability; a shorter description reduces invocations instead of fixing the problem.

questions.q: A library migration will touch roughly 45 files across an unfamiliar codebase. How should the work start?
options: In planning mode, exploring safely and producing a plan to approve
By running the migration on a branch and reviewing the whole diff after
In direct execution, fixing files one at a time as they come up
By delegating the whole migration to a single autonomous subagent
questions.explain: Large changes with several viable approaches in unfamiliar code are the plan-mode case: it explores without side effects and produces a plan a person approves before anything is touched. Direct execution is for single-file fixes with a clear cause; running it on a branch and reviewing the diff afterwards discovers the problems after making them; handing the whole migration to one subagent delegates the architectural decision.

questions.q: Which TWO statements about the built-in /compact and /memory commands are correct? (Select 2)
options: Compacting can lose numeric values and dates in the summary
Compacting is required before any session can exceed its window
Memory entries apply only to the session where they were written
Facts recorded in memory files (edited via /memory) load automatically in later sessions
Compacting keeps every message verbatim in the model's context and only hides it from the display
questions.explain: Compaction frees the window by compressing history, and concrete details — figures, dates, names — can be lost in that compression. What is saved as memory lives in CLAUDE.md files and loads automatically at the start of later sessions. Compaction replaces the history in context with a summary, so the original text is no longer available to the model; memory is not limited to one session (that would defeat its purpose); compaction is not a prerequisite for anything.

questions.q: An extraction step must return a consistent output shape. Prose instructions describing the format keep producing variations. What works better?
options: Two to four worked input and output examples in the prompt
A longer written description of the format
A reminder at the end of the prompt to respect the format
A lower temperature so the output varies less between runs
questions.explain: Two to four worked input/output examples beat any written description for format consistency, and the model generalises the pattern to new cases rather than copying the examples. A longer description and a closing reminder both keep describing instead of showing; a lower temperature reduces variation but does not teach the expected shape.

questions.q: A review prompt says 'be conservative and report only high-confidence findings'. Results are inconsistent between runs. What is the defect?
options: The model needs a larger context to be consistent about it
Confidence cannot really be expressed in a prompt in any useful way
The criterion is vague, so each run interprets it differently
The prompt is too short for the model to apply judgement
questions.explain: 'Conservative' and 'high confidence' are not criteria. Define exactly what to flag, what not to flag and what each severity level means, with an example per level. Blaming prompt length or context size mistakes ambiguity for size; confidence can be expressed in a prompt — through explicit criteria — so 'it cannot be expressed' is false.

questions.q: Which TWO uses of the tool_choice parameter are correct? (Select 2)
options: Setting it to any when the model should be free to answer in text
Setting it to any when a structured result must always come back
Setting it to auto when the output must always be structured
Forcing a specific tool to stop the model from hallucinating facts
Forcing a specific tool when execution order has to be enforced
questions.explain: any forces the model to call some tool, which guarantees a structured result; forcing a specific tool enforces execution order. auto is the opposite of a guarantee — it lets the model answer in text, which is also why 'any when the model should be free to answer in text' describes auto, not any; forcing a tool controls which tool is called, not whether the facts are hallucinated. Nota sobre el modelo: forzar una herramienta con tool_choice any/tool funciona en los modelos que lo admiten, pero Claude Opus 5.5 lo rechaza con un error 400. En Opus 5.5, usa auto con uso estricto de herramientas (strict tool use) o salidas estructuradas. Fuente: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/opus-5-5/migration-guide

questions.q: An extraction schema marks every field as required. Documents that lack a field come back with invented values. What is the fix?
options: Split the schema so each field is extracted in its own call
Reject any extraction where a required field looks implausible
Make fields that may be absent optional or explicitly nullable
Add an instruction telling the model never to invent values
questions.explain: A required field forces the model to put something there. Mark as required only what is always available; everything else is optional or nullable. An instruction never to invent values asks in text for the opposite of what the schema demands; rejecting implausible values detects the problem late and by hand; one call per field multiplies calls without fixing the cause.

questions.q: A classification enum keeps forcing borderline documents into the closest available category. What design change helps?
options: Instruct the model to pick the category it considers most likely
Raise the temperature so the classification is less rigid
Add an unclear value, plus an other option with a detail field
Add more categories until every observed document fits one
questions.explain: An 'unclear' value is better than a wrong category, and an 'other' with a detail field keeps the schema extensible without inventing categories. Adding categories chases an infinite tail; telling the model to pick the most likely category is exactly what it is already doing wrong; temperature has nothing to do with the enum design.

questions.q: Invoice totals occasionally disagree with the sum of their line items, and nothing downstream notices. Which extraction design surfaces it?
options: Extract only the stated total, since it is what the document says
Round both values so small differences stop being reported
Extract only the calculated total, since it is the trustworthy one
Extract the stated total and the calculated total, and flag conflicts
questions.explain: Extracting both the stated and the calculated total and flagging the conflict turns a silent discrepancy into data someone can resolve. Keeping only the calculated total, or only the stated one, picks a side and loses the signal; rounding both hides the problem.

questions.q: Which TWO statements about the Message Batches API are correct? (Select 2)
options: It costs around half of the equivalent synchronous calls
It guarantees a response within a fixed low-latency window
It runs the tool and continues the loop on its own inside a single batch entry
The whole batch must be resubmitted if any single entry fails
Requests are correlated to their responses by a custom identifier
questions.explain: Batches save about 50% and use your own custom_id to pair each request with its response. The processing window is up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee, so a low-latency guarantee is wrong. A batch entry is one request and one response, so no tool loop runs inside it; and only the failed entries are resubmitted (in a new batch), not the whole batch.

questions.q: Two tools share the description 'Retrieves information' and the agent keeps picking the wrong one. What fixes it?
options: Remove one of the two tools from the agent's catalogue
Merge both tools into one that takes a mode parameter
Rename each tool and state the concrete data each one returns
Add an instruction telling the model to think before choosing
questions.explain: The description is the selection mechanism. A specific name plus the concrete data each tool returns removes the ambiguity at its root. Telling the model to think first adds latency without removing the ambiguity; merging into one tool with a mode parameter hides the decision inside a parameter; removing a tool sacrifices a capability that is in use.

questions.q: An MCP tool fails. Which TWO elements should its error response carry so the coordinator can recover intelligently? (Select 2)
options: The full stack trace of the underlying service failure
The total number of times this tool has failed this week
A flag stating whether retrying the call could succeed
A generic message saying the operation could not be completed
A category such as transient, validation, permission or business
questions.explain: The coordinator needs to know what kind of failure occurred and whether retrying could help; with that it decides between backoff, fixing the input, proposing an alternative or escalating. A full stack trace is noise to the model; a generic 'could not complete' message is the anti-pattern that prevents recovery; a weekly failure count is an operations metric, not information about this call.

questions.q: A project's MCP server needs an API token, and the configuration file is committed to the repository. How is that handled?
options: Reference an environment variable from the configuration file
Keep the whole configuration out of version control instead
Commit the token and rotate it whenever someone leaves
Store the token in the project CLAUDE.md so it is documented
questions.explain: Project configuration is committed with environment-variable expansion: the file travels to the repository, the token does not. Committing the token and rotating it publishes the secret; keeping the whole configuration out of version control loses the benefit of sharing it; putting the token in CLAUDE.md also puts it in the context window.

questions.q: A developer wants to try an MCP server on their own, without affecting teammates. Where does that configuration go?
options: In the project configuration, disabled by default
In a branch of the repository that is never merged
In the project configuration, with a comment explaining it
In the user-level configuration in their home directory
questions.explain: User-level configuration lives in the developer's home directory, is not shared through version control, and is the place to experiment without affecting the team. Adding it to the project configuration — disabled, or with a comment — still pollutes the shared configuration; a never-merged branch is something to keep alive for no reason.

questions.q: An agent burns several tool calls each session just discovering what data is available. What reduces that?
options: Increase the agent's context so it can remember prior sessions
Add a tool that lists every other tool and what it does
Expose a resource that maps the available data up front
Instruct the agent to guess the structure before querying
questions.explain: A resource that provides the catalogue or schema gives the agent the map up front and saves the exploratory calls spent discovering what could have been declared. A bigger context does not persist between sessions; a tool that lists the other tools describes tools, not data; telling the agent to guess invites invention.

questions.q: In a long support conversation, the order number and the amount keep getting lost after the history is summarised. What fixes it?
options: Keep a case-facts block outside the history and resend it every turn
Summarise less aggressively so more of the history survives
Ask the model to repeat the key facts at the end of each reply
Raise the context window so summarisation happens later
questions.explain: If a fact must survive no matter what, it cannot live only in the conversation. A case-facts block is kept separately, updated, and re-injected with every request. Summarising less aggressively and enlarging the window only postpone the problem; asking the model to repeat the facts leaves persistence in the model's own hands.

questions.q: A long input is processed reliably at the beginning and the end, but details in the middle are missed. What is the mitigation?
options: Place the decisive information near the start or the end
Increase the temperature so more of the input is considered
Split the input into random chunks and process them apart
Repeat the whole input twice so the middle appears elsewhere
questions.explain: The lost-in-the-middle effect is well known and is mitigated by position: what decides the answer goes near the start or the end. Repeating the whole input doubles the cost; temperature has nothing to do with it; random chunks destroy the document's order.

questions.q: Which TWO are reliable triggers for escalating to a human? (Select 2)
options: The sentiment analysis scores the message as angry
The customer explicitly asks to speak with a person
The conversation has exceeded a fixed number of turns
The model reports low confidence in its own answer
The request falls into a gap the policy does not cover
questions.explain: An explicit request and a policy gap are unambiguous signals. The rest are unreliable proxies: sentiment is not the same as complexity, and the model can be confidently wrong. An angry sentiment score confuses emotion with difficulty; self-reported low confidence is uncalibrated self-assessment; a fixed turn count is an arbitrary threshold.

questions.q: A long investigation will span several sessions. How are the findings preserved?
options: Keep the session open indefinitely so nothing is ever lost
Rely on compaction to retain the important parts of the history
Write key findings to a file and reference it in the next session
Repeat the discovery steps at the start of each new session
questions.explain: A notes file survives context degradation and the end of a session, and avoids repeating discovery from scratch. Keeping a session open indefinitely is not sustainable; compaction loses exactly the concrete details; repeating the discovery steps each session wastes time and tokens.

questions.q: A subagent partly fails. Which TWO elements should its structured response include so the synthesis stays honest? (Select 2)
options: The number of retries it performed before giving up entirely
An empty result set so the coordinator can move on quickly
A note on what coverage was lost because of the failure
The partial results it did manage to gather before failing
A recommendation that the whole workflow be aborted
questions.explain: Deliver what you have and declare the gap: partial results plus a coverage annotation let the synthesis proceed without pretending the material is complete. Recommending that the whole workflow abort throws away valid work; an empty result set is a silent failure; the retry count is an operational detail that does not change the synthesis.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline routes high-confidence results straight through. How do you know the confidence scores can be trusted?
options: Audit a stratified sample of them and measure accuracy by field
Ask the model to re-rate the confidence of its own extractions
Raise the threshold until the volume of errors becomes acceptable
Review every low-confidence case and assume the rest are fine
questions.explain: Confidence is calibrated against reality: a stratified sample, with accuracy measured by document type and by field, not just in aggregate. Asking the model to re-rate its confidence is self-assessment again; raising the threshold moves it without evidence; reviewing only the low-confidence cases assumes exactly what had to be verified about the high-confidence ones.

questions.q: A tool returns forty fields but the task only ever uses five. What reduces the noise it adds to context?
options: Trim the result to the needed fields before it enters the context
Call the tool less often so the noise accumulates slower
Increase the context window to absorb the extra fields
Ask the model to ignore the fields that are not relevant
questions.explain: Trimming the result before it enters the context cuts noise and tokens at once — deterministic work that belongs to the system, not the model. Asking the model to ignore fields still pays for them in context; a bigger window just moves the problem; calling the tool less often reduces its usefulness.

questions.q: An assistant handles two kinds of request: simple status lookups that arrive constantly, and complex disputes that need deep analysis. Which design serves both?
options: A router that classifies the request and sends it down the fitting path
Two separate products, each with its own interface and its own login
One agent with every tool available, deciding what to do per request
A single prompt long enough to cover lookups and disputes together
questions.explain: When inputs fall into clearly distinct categories, classifying first and routing lets simple requests be served cheaply and quickly while reserving deep analysis for what needs it. One agent with every tool pays the complex case's cost on every trivial lookup; a single long prompt mixes two tasks; two separate products split the user experience for no reason.

questions.q: A pipeline extracts data, transforms it and writes it to a system of record. Where does validation belong?
options: After each step, so a bad result never reaches the following one
At the very end, right before the write to the system of record
Only at the start, validating the input document that arrived
Nowhere: the model is instructed to check its own work as it goes
questions.explain: Validating between steps is what makes a chain debuggable: an error is caught where it originates and does not contaminate what follows. It is the main reason to decompose. Validating only at the end catches errors after they have propagated; validating only the input misses what the process itself generates; trusting the model to check itself leaves the guarantee to an instruction.

questions.q: In a four-stage chain, the third stage fails on about one request in twenty. What belongs in the design?
options: A fifth stage that reviews the output and repairs whatever looks wrong
A larger model in stage three so the failures become less frequent
A defined behaviour for that failure: retry, fall back, or stop and report
A rule telling the model to skip stage three when it cannot complete
questions.explain: A production chain needs defined behaviour on failure, not just a happy path. Retry, fallback or an explicit stop are design decisions made beforehand, not during the incident. A repair stage patches downstream without knowing what failed; a larger model lowers the frequency but still does not define what happens when it fails; silently skipping stage three drops a needed step.

questions.q: A classification task has eight well-defined categories and clear written definitions for each. Accuracy is already high without examples. What follows?
options: Add few-shot examples anyway, since they always improve accuracy
Add one example per category as a precaution, without any measured need
Move to a larger model to protect the accuracy already achieved
Keep it zero-shot and add examples only if measured errors appear
questions.explain: Examples cost tokens on every request. If the definitions already suffice and accuracy is high, adding examples pays a cost and buys nothing, so keeping it zero-shot, and adding examples only where errors are measured, is the right call; each technique is applied according to measured benefit. 'Examples always improve accuracy' is an absolute rule that does not hold; one example per category inflates the prompt without evidence of need; a larger model spends capability where there is no problem.

questions.q: A support conversation runs long and the earliest messages start falling out of the window. What preserves quality?
options: Summarise the older turns and keep the decisive facts verbatim
Move to the model with the largest window and keep everything
Let the oldest turns drop, since recent context matters more
Start a new conversation whenever the window gets close to full
questions.explain: Summarising the older turns while keeping the decisive facts — identifiers, amounts, commitments — verbatim does both jobs: it fits the window and keeps the data whose absence would break the answer. Letting the oldest turns drop discards information without judgement; a bigger window only defers the problem a few turns; starting a new conversation loses the thread.

questions.q: An internal API exposes forty endpoints. The team is deciding how to expose it to the agent. What should drive the tool boundaries?
options: One tool per endpoint, so the whole surface stays available to it
A single tool that receives the endpoint name and its parameters
The endpoints the backend team considers most stable over time
The tasks the agent needs to accomplish, not the endpoints that exist
questions.explain: Tools are designed per task. Mirroring the internal API pushes its complexity onto the model, which handles it worst; grouped by task, the complexity stays on the deterministic side. One tool per endpoint gives the agent too many capabilities to choose from; a single generic tool throws away typed interfaces; backend stability is a backend criterion applied to an agent-design decision.

questions.q: A developer joins a team that works with AI assistance daily. What gets them productive fastest?
options: The shared project configuration and standards the team already uses
A training session covering prompt techniques and their trade-offs
Read-only access for the first weeks, until they know the codebase
Their own configuration, so they can work the way they prefer
questions.explain: Shared, version-controlled project configuration is the onboarding mechanism: the new developer inherits proven practice on day one without depending on someone explaining it. A prompt-technique course teaches technique without the team's context; weeks of read-only access postpone productivity; their own private configuration recreates fragmentation.

questions.q: An AI coding assistant needs access to a service that requires an API key. How is that handled?
options: A configuration file kept out of the repository through the ignore list
A note in the project documentation explaining where to find the key
A key with a short expiry, pasted into the session when it is needed
An environment variable the tooling reads, never a file under version control
questions.explain: Secrets live in environment variables that the configuration references. Everything else eventually ends up inside a repository or a context window. A git-ignored config file depends on nobody ever slipping once; a documentation note just records where the secret is; pasting a short-lived key into the session puts it in the model's context.
